entries: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?
George Eliot, Middlemarch, Book VIII, chapter 72 (Dorothea)
Fiction
No man is devoid of a heart sensitive to the suffering of others.
Mencius, Mencius, Book II, Part A, 6 (trans. D. C. Lau, 1970)
Philosophy

Then it is only kindness that makes sense anymore, / only kindness that ties your shoes / and sends you out into the day to mail letters and purchase bread, / only kindness that raises its head / from the crowd of the world to say / It is I you have been looking for, / and then goes with you everywhere / like a shadow or a friend.
Naomi Shihab Nye, Kindness, closing eight lines, Words Under the Words (Far Corner Books, 1995); first in Different Ways to Pray (1980)
Poetry
I am a man, and nothing that concerns a man do I deem a matter of indifference to me.
Terence, Heauton Timorumenos, Act 1, scene 1, line 77 (Chremes) (trans. Henry Thomas Riley, 1853)
Drama
Ultimately, we have just one moral duty: to reclaim large areas of peace in ourselves, more and more peace, and to reflect it toward others.
Etty Hillesum, An Interrupted Life, diary, 29 September 1942 (trans. Arnold J. Pomerans, 1983; Holt, 1996, p. 218)
Diary

The wording is the Henry Holt 1996 printing of Pomerans, p. 218, with the comma and toward; the 1983 Pantheon printing reads towards and no comma. The page itself was not opened; the entry date rests on every dated reproduction of the passage.
His little, nameless, unremembered acts / Of kindness and of love.
William Wordsworth, Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey, lines 35 to 36, Lyrical Ballads (J. and A. Arch, 1798)
Poetry

Wording verified in the 1798 Lyrical Ballads text, where a comma follows unremembered in no copy consulted. In the 1798 numbering, with the half line Though absent long counted with the line before it, these are lines 35 and 36; the standard later text numbers them 34 and 35.
Compassion is the chief law of human existence.
Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Idiot, Part II, chapter 5 (Prince Myshkin, in thought) (trans. Eva Martin, 1913)
Fiction
The love of our neighbor in all its fullness simply means being able to say to him: ‘What are you going through?’
Simone Weil, Waiting for God, Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies, p. 115 (trans. Emma Craufurd, 1951)
Essay
The quality of mercy is not strained. / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven / Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest: / It blesseth him that gives and him that takes.
William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, scene 1, lines 190 to 193, Folger edition (Portia)
Drama
Little feet of children / blue with cold, / how can they see you and not cover you— / dear God!
Gabriela Mistral, Piececitos (Little Feet), lines 1 to 4, Selected Poems of Gabriela Mistral (trans. Doris Dana, 1971)
Poetry
The best way to begin a day well is to think, on awakening, whether we cannot give pleasure during the day to at least one person.
Friedrich Nietzsche, Human, All-Too-Human, vol. I, section 589, The Day’s First Thought (trans. Helen Zimmern, 1909)
Philosophy
You never really understand a person until you consider things from his point of view … until you climb into his skin and walk around in it.
Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird, Part One, chapter 3 (Atticus Finch)
Fiction
The spaced ellipsis stands for Scout’s interjection, Sir?, and the two dashes around it in the novel; every word is Lee’s.
Don’t kill that fly! / Look—it’s wringing its hands, / wringing its feet.
Kobayashi Issa, ‘Don’t kill that fly!’, The Essential Haiku, Issa section (trans. Robert Hass, 1994)
Poetry
There is no charm equal to tenderness of heart.
Jane Austen, Emma, Volume II, chapter 13 (Emma Woodhouse, to herself)
Fiction
All the joy the world contains / Has come through wishing happiness for others. / All the misery the world contains / Has come through wanting pleasure for oneself.
Shantideva, The Way of the Bodhisattva, chapter 8, verse 129 (trans. Padmakara Translation Group, rev. ed. 2006)
Philosophy
I feel at home in the entire world, wherever there are clouds and birds and human tears.
Rosa Luxemburg, letter to Mathilde Wurm, 16 February 1917, from Wronke; The Letters of Rosa Luxemburg, p. 376 (trans. George Shriver, 2011)
Correspondence

The comma after world is restored to Shriver’s Verso text as three reviewers quote it; Nettl’s 1966 rendering prints the sentence without it. In the letter the sentence closes a rebuke of sorrow kept for one people only; alone it is the universal line.
Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.
Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre, chapter 6 (Helen Burns)
Fiction

If I can stop one heart from breaking, / I shall not live in vain; / If I can ease one life the aching, / Or cool one pain, / Or help one fainting robin / Unto his nest again, / I shall not live in vain.
Emily Dickinson, ‘If I can stop one heart from breaking’ (Fr982, J919), Poems, ed. Todd and Higginson (Roberts Brothers, 1890), Life VI
Poetry
’Tis not my nature to join in hating, but in loving.
Sophocles, Antigone, line 523 (Antigone) (trans. R. C. Jebb, 1891)
Drama
She is a friend of my mind. She gather me, man. The pieces I am, she gather them and give them back to me in all the right order.
Toni Morrison, Beloved, Part Three (Knopf, 1987, pp. 272 to 273) (Sixo, remembered by Paul D)
Fiction
Sixo’s words for the Thirty-Mile Woman, as Paul D remembers them to Sethe in the last pages of Part Three: a reported line, and the reporter is named.
Boundless compassion for all living beings is the surest and most certain guarantee of pure moral conduct, and needs no casuistry.
Arthur Schopenhauer, The Basis of Morality, Part III, Chapter VIII, (4) (trans. Arthur Brodrick Bullock, 1903)
Philosophy
Warning, in music-words / devout and large, / that we are each other’s / harvest: / we are each other’s / business: / we are each other’s / magnitude and bond.
Gwendolyn Brooks, Paul Robeson, lines 10 to 17, the closing lines, Family Pictures (Broadside Press, 1970)
Poetry
I have learnt that all men live not by care for themselves but by love.
Leo Tolstoy, What Men Live By, section XII (the angel Michael) (trans. Louise and Aylmer Maude, 1906)
Fiction
Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real.
Iris Murdoch, The Sublime and the Good, Chicago Review 13.3 (1959), p. 51; in Existentialists and Mystics (1997), p. 215
Essay
He drew a circle that shut me out — / Heretic, rebel, a thing to flout. / But Love and I had the wit to win: / We drew a circle that took him in!
Edwin Markham, Outwitted, the whole poem, p. 1 (Voluntaries), The Shoes of Happiness, and Other Poems (Doubleday, Page, 1915)
Poetry

The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is.
Marcel Proust, The Captive, chapter II, the Vinteuil septet (trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff, 1929)
Fiction

Scott Moncrieff’s sentence runs on after a semicolon: and this we can contrive with an Elstir, with a Vinteuil. The line is cut at that clause and given a full stop; every word is his, and the fountain of Eternal Youth is his own flourish, absent from the French.
All real living is meeting.
Martin Buber, I and Thou, Part One, p. 11 (trans. Ronald Gregor Smith, 1937)
Philosophy
There is always something left to love. And if you ain’t learned that, you ain’t learned nothing.
Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun, Act III (Random House, 1959) (Mama, Lena Younger)
Drama
There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.
Thornton Wilder, The Bridge of San Luis Rey, Part Five: Perhaps an Intention, closing sentence (the Abbess, in thought)
Fiction

unused.quote: Travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness, and many of our people need it sorely on these accounts. Broad, wholesome, charitable views of men and things can not be acquired by vegetating in one little corner of the earth all one’s lifetime.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Innocents Abroad, Conclusion (American Publishing Company, 1869)
unused.note: Verified in the 1869 first edition, p. 650; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 1. A road line more than a kindness line.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: CORRECTED: the sentence is in The Return, Part II, not The Scot Abroad. The real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 36. A road line.

unused.quote: Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
unused.source: Ian Fleming, Casino Royale, chapter 20, The Nature of Evil (Jonathan Cape, 1953) (René Mathis)
unused.note: Verified in the chapter text; people over abstractions, spoken by Mathis. A service line.

unused.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified with the two-word for ever; the Calendar For Life copy modernised it. Only one Tolkien may land in a month and the bank carries many.

unused.quote: If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, chapter 18, The Return Journey (George Allen and Unwin, 1937) (Thorin Oakenshield)
unused.note: Verified in Thorin’s farewell; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 511. A gratitude line.

unused.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
unused.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, Part One, The Rebel (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
unused.note: Verified in Bower with his em dash, the last sentence of Part One; the real text behind Calendar For Life candidate 3. Camus stands at one for the year.

unused.quote: There is no religion without love, and people may talk as much as they like about their religion, but if it does not teach them to be good and kind to man and beast it is all a sham.
unused.source: Anna Sewell, Black Beauty, Part I, chapter 13 (John Manly)
unused.note: CORRECTED: Sewell’s sentence runs on, all a sham, James, and it won’t stand when things come to be turned inside out; the line is cut at the clause and given a full stop, and the first word is raised to a capital.

unused.quote: As far as the education of children is concerned I think they should be taught not the little virtues but the great ones. Not thrift but generosity and an indifference to money; not caution but courage and a contempt for danger; nor shrewdness but frankness and a love of truth; not tact but love for one’s neighbour and self-denial; not a desire for success but a desire to be and to know.
unused.source: Natalia Ginzburg, The Little Virtues, title essay, 1960, opening sentences (trans. Dick Davis, 1985)
unused.note: CORRECTED to the book’s nor shrewdness; the anthologies smooth it to not, and PN Review 44 (1985) printed Davis with not and a differently worded first sentence. A counsel line.

unused.quote: Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business.
unused.source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave One (Jacob Marley’s Ghost)
unused.note: Verified in Stave One with the first-edition commas. A December line by its book.

unused.quote: Let the tears of the poor man find with thee more compassion, but not more justice, than the pleadings of the rich.
unused.source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 42 (Don Quixote, to Sancho Panza) (trans. John Ormsby, 1885)
unused.note: Verified in Ormsby. Compassion tempered by justice: a September line.

unused.quote: If a man should importune me to give a reason why I loved him, I find it could no otherwise be expressed, than by making answer: because it was he, because it was I.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, chapter 27, Of Friendship (trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified in Cotton and Hazlitt, whose numbering is 27 (28 in Villey). January routed Montaigne’s good faith to June; one Montaigne per month.

unused.quote: You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed.
unused.source: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, The Little Prince, chapter XXI (the fox) (trans. Katherine Woods, 1943)
unused.note: Verified in Woods, the fox’s own line. A responsibility line.

unused.quote: It is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world!
unused.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4 (1792)
unused.note: Verified in the 1792 text. Reads as the corrective to a compassion month, and is the September line itself. January routed a different Wollstonecraft line to March.

unused.quote: The good we secure for ourselves is precarious and uncertain, is floating in mid-air, until it is secured for all of us and incorporated into our common life.
unused.source: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, Chapter VI, The Subjective Necessity for Social Settlements (Macmillan, 1910)
unused.note: Verified in the 1910 text and the 1893 Crowell printing of the paper; a lifted final clause with its first letter raised, every word in order.

unused.quote: The greatest benefit we owe to the artist, whether painter, poet, or novelist, is the extension of our sympathies.
unused.source: George Eliot, The Natural History of German Life, Westminster Review, July 1856; in Essays of George Eliot, ed. Sheppard (1883), essay V
unused.note: Verified twice in the Sheppard edition; refuted only as a month collision with the Middlemarch line, which landed. Eliot stands at two for the year after February.

unused.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
unused.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
unused.note: Verified in Frechtman. Beauvoir stands at one for the year.

unused.quote: Forgiving, in other words, is the only reaction which does not merely re-act but acts anew and unexpectedly, unconditioned by the act which provoked it and therefore freeing from its consequences both the one who forgives and the one who is forgiven.
unused.source: Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, chapter V, section 33, Irreversibility and the Power to Forgive (Chicago, 1958), p. 241
unused.note: Verified against the Chicago text. Arendt stands at one for the year; forgiveness as beginning anew is a December line.

unused.quote: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
unused.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, Section I, Chapter I, Of Sympathy (6th edition, 1790)
unused.note: Verified: the opening sentence of the book in the 6th edition.

unused.quote: Yet minds are not conquered by force, but by love and high-mindedness.
unused.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Appendix, XI (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
unused.note: Verified in Elwes. January routed Spinoza’s closing sentence to March; one Spinoza per month.

unused.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
unused.source: Bertrand Russell, What I Believe, chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), p. 20
unused.note: Verified in the 1925 Dutton text, italicised as his creed. A counsel line.

unused.quote: You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat.
unused.source: George Herbert, Love (III), lines 17 to 18, The Temple (Cambridge, 1633)
unused.note: Verified in two copies of the 1633 printing, closing couplet of the last poem of The Church. A gratitude line.

unused.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
unused.source: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market, lines 562 to 567, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862) (Laura)
unused.note: Verified, the closing lines of the poem. Lifting one who totters is a trial line.

unused.quote: Here is thy footstool and there rest thy feet where live the poorest, and lowliest, and lost.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 10, opening sentence (the author’s own English, 1912)
unused.note: Verified in the Macmillan text; a prose poem, so no line breaks. January routed Light, my light to December; one Tagore per month.

unused.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
unused.source: Adrienne Rich, Natural Resources, closing six lines, The Dream of a Common Language (W. W. Norton, 1978)
unused.note: Verified against three postings crediting the 1978 edition; the Norton page itself was not opened. A trial line.

unused.quote: Somebody loves us all.
unused.source: Elizabeth Bishop, Filling Station, closing line, Questions of Travel (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965)
unused.note: Verified, the closing line of the poem; four words, a very bare card. A gratitude line.

unused.quote: You do not have to be good. / You do not have to walk on your knees / for a hundred miles through the desert repenting. / You only have to let the soft animal of your body / love what it loves.
unused.source: Mary Oliver, Wild Geese, lines 1 to 5, Dream Work (Atlantic Monthly Press, 1986), p. 14
unused.note: Verified against reprints crediting Dream Work, no comma before repenting; later printings add one. A renewal line.

unused.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
unused.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (trans. Raymond Rosenthal, 1976, in Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, p. 462)
unused.note: Carried from January and held again: February took Weil’s What are you going through?, verified on the page, and one Weil per month. Page 462 rests on four scholarly citations. An attention line.

unused.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
unused.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
unused.note: Carried from January, verified in Carson, p. 27. Before it lands, the four lines must be marked with slashes in Carson’s lineation, which nobody has yet checked against the page; it is carried as prose.

report.thinnestLane: Diary (one survivor in the whole month, the Hillesum line, proposed by two lanes); Correspondence next (two survivors, both usable, one Weil, so one may land)
